clinicalPearls: A congenital synkinesis in which a ptotic upper eyelid elevates on movement of the jaw, classically when the mouth opens or the jaw moves to the opposite side
Reflects anomalous connections between the motor branch of the trigeminal nerve supplying the pterygoid muscles and the levator palpebrae superioris
Usually unilateral and present from birth, often noticed during bottle or breast feeding as the lid flickers with sucking
The underlying ptosis in primary position must be assessed separately, as it determines amblyogenic risk and surgical planning
Amblyopia can arise from the ptosis itself, associated anisometropia or strabismus rather than the winking
The winking movement tends to persist even after ptosis surgery unless the synkinetic levator is addressed
For significant cases, surgery may involve levator disinsertion with frontalis suspension, sometimes bilaterally for symmetry
reference.pathophysiology: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking is a congenital trigemino-oculomotor synkinesis caused by aberrant innervation, in which fibres of the motor division of the trigeminal nerve destined for the pterygoid muscles are misdirected to the levator palpebrae superioris. As a result, activation of the jaw muscles simultaneously produces contraction of the levator, so the ptotic lid rises when the mouth opens or the jaw deviates. The baseline ptosis reflects the abnormal levator innervation, and the synkinetic elevation is an involuntary, stimulus-linked movement. Because the anomaly is at the level of nerve wiring, the winking is not abolished by conventional levator-strengthening surgery alone.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital third nerve palsy with aberrant regeneration
Inverse (Marin-Amat) synkinesis with lid closure on jaw movement
additionalInvestigations: Observation of lid movement during sucking, chewing or lateral jaw excursion
Measurement of levator function and ptosis in primary position
Cycloplegic refraction and amblyopia and strabismus assessment
Orthoptic evaluation for associated ocular deviation
Assessment of the excursion and stimulus of the wink to gauge severity
Preoperative planning of the affected levator and any bilateral surgery
redFlags: Amblyopia from ptosis, anisometropia or strabismus needing prompt treatment
A large or cosmetically and socially troublesome wink causing functional impact
Associated ophthalmoplegia or pupil signs suggesting a third nerve process
Fatigable ptosis raising the possibility of myasthenia
reference.prognosis: The synkinesis is stable and benign, and outcomes are generally good when amblyopia is managed and surgery is appropriately selected, though residual asymmetry or persistence of the wink can occur if the synkinetic levator is not addressed.
pitfalls: Correcting the ptosis without addressing the synkinetic levator, leaving a persistent wink
Missing associated amblyopia, anisometropia or strabismus
Failing to observe feeding or jaw movement and overlooking the diagnosis
Confusing it with aberrant third nerve regeneration
references: Taylor & Hoyt's Paediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
